heading: PROPHET ʿĪSĀ (AS)
title: THE MESSAGE OF TRUTH AND MERCY
themes: Tawḥīd • Truthfulness • Dignity • Prayer • Compassion • Trust • Service • Hope
scope: 8 CONNECTED STORIES | 12 INTERACTIVE MISSIONS | 16 SELECTED QUR’ANIC VERSES
reviewNote: Editorial working edition • Qualified muṣḥaf, English meaning, Sunni classical Tafsīr and child-safeguarding review required before release.
introduction: Volume Twenty-Four continues directly from Prophet Yaḥyā (AS). The previous world closes by introducing the next name: ʿĪsā ibn Maryam (AS). We now teach the honoured Messenger whom Allah created without a father, a sign and mercy to people, whose words and miracles were by Allah’s permission, and who consistently called people to worship Allah alone. The Qur’an rejects the claims that he was killed or crucified and states that Allah raised him to Himself. We teach the Islamic creed faithfully, while never training a child to mock or harm people who hold other beliefs.

This volume is rooted in Āl ʿImrān 3:42–55, Maryam 19:16–36, al-Māʾidah 5:110–120, al-Nisāʾ 4:157–158, and al-Ṣaff 61:6 and 61:14. These passages are interpreted within established Sunni Tafsīr. The public source library below selects sixteen complete āyāt in working Arabic script; contextual verses remain identified in source notes. The approved production version must use an independently checked Arabic muṣḥaf, a reviewed English translation and qualified scholarly approval.

blocks.text: The blue folder marked YAḤYĀ still rested on Sheikh Uncle’s library table. Imaan had returned it after the academy exhibit, but Akhlaq had noticed that its final page did not quite lie flat. Something had been tucked between the pages.

He pulled out a card bearing another name: ʿĪSĀ IBN MARYAM. “Is he the next Prophet we will learn about?” he asked. Dadi Jaan smiled. “Yes. Last time we learned that the Qur’an names Zakariyyā, Yaḥyā, ʿĪsā and Ilyās among the righteous. Today we begin a different account, one in which Maryam has a special place.”

Akhlaq knew that Maryam was honoured in the Qur’an. Imaan opened Āl ʿImrān 3:42 and listened as Dadi explained Allah’s choosing and purifying her. They did not draw Maryam, stage the speech of an angel, or pretend to watch a sacred moment. Instead, they wrote a careful source label: WHAT THE QUR’AN TELLS US.

Their academy was preparing a new learning gallery called THE TRUSTED STORY. Sir Zameer asked each team to create a display that would distinguish authentic information from an attractive guess. Mohsin hurried to find dramatic pictures online. “Everybody will stop at our table if it looks mysterious,” he argued. Mohsina asked how they would know whether the pictures told the truth.

Akhlaq almost agreed with Mohsin. He loved a puzzle. Yet he remembered the previous volume’s lesson: a good question deserved a checked answer, not a confident invention. He returned the pictures and suggested using a labelled Qur’an stand, a family-relationship card and a timeline made only of events established by revelation.

When Sheikh Uncle visited the group, he did not praise its decoration first. “What does your audience leave believing?” he asked. Imaan pointed to their opening sentence: Allah honoured Maryam, and the account of her son is to be learned from revelation. “Then your design has begun in the right place,” he replied.
At home Akhlaq placed the new name beside Yaḥyā. The card did not complete the mystery. It began a responsibility: before telling a remarkable story, make sure it is true.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Protect the dignity of sacred teaching: learn the authentic account before decorating it.

stories.title: The Good News and the Difficult Question
stories.subtitle: Hope does not grant us knowledge of the unseen

blocks.text: A visitor arrived at the academy with a large box of art materials. The school had received a donation for its new reading corner, and the children were delighted. Akhlaq began planning a celebration before they had even counted the supplies. “Now every class will have exactly everything it needs!” he announced.

Sir Zameer gently asked him to pause. The donation was real and welcome; the future supply of every classroom was not something Akhlaq knew. The team could thank the donor, check what had arrived and plan how to share it fairly.

That afternoon Dadi Jaan opened Āl ʿImrān 3:45–47. She explained the glad tidings given to Maryam of ʿĪsā, son of Maryam. Maryam asked how she could have a child when no man had touched her. The Qur’an answers that Allah creates what He wills. The birth of ʿĪsā without a father was an extraordinary sign from Allah, not an ordinary event that people can arrange or claim for themselves.
“Was her question wrong?” Imaan asked.

“No,” replied Dadi. “The Qur’an records the question. We must teach what the passage says rather than inventing fears or conversations beyond it. A sincere question asked with respect is different from claiming to know what Allah has not told us.”

At school the group counted the donated materials. There were enough for several class packs, but not yet enough for every pupil to take a complete set home. Mohsin looked disappointed. Akhlaq was quiet for a moment and then proposed a lending schedule. Imaan suggested telling the school the truth about what was available instead of making a magnificent but misleading announcement.

On their display Akhlaq wrote: GRATITUDE IS TRUE EVEN WHEN A PLAN MUST CHANGE. At home, he explained to Salaam that he had confused a hopeful wish with a guaranteed result. Salaam reminded him that Allah’s special glad tidings to Maryam are revelation; our everyday duty is to thank Allah, act honestly and acknowledge what we do not know.
The new gallery had not yet opened, but the children had already learned to protect a beautiful truth from exaggeration.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Thank Allah for genuine blessings while speaking honestly about unknown outcomes.

stories.title: The Rumour on the Noticeboard
stories.subtitle: Protecting dignity by refusing unsupported accusations

blocks.text: On Monday, a message appeared on the academy noticeboard: SOMEONE IN TEAM AMANAH HAS HIDDEN THE PRESENTATION CARDS. Nobody had signed the note, but several pupils quickly decided the new student must be responsible. A whisper passed from table to table until even those who had seen nothing were repeating the accusation.

Mohsina came to Imaan with an uneasy expression. “The cards are missing,” she said, “but I cannot find a single person who actually saw anyone take them.” Imaan asked Sir Zameer for help. The teacher checked the storage room, the project shelves and the record of materials moved for cleaning. The cards were in a folder taken to another classroom for lamination. The new student had not hidden anything.

That evening, Dadi Jaan explained Sūrah Maryam 19:27–34. Maryam faced serious accusations when she returned carrying her infant. By Allah’s miracle the baby ʿĪsā spoke, declaring himself Allah’s servant and a Prophet. The children were not asked to imitate that miracle, compare their school confusion to Maryam’s trial, or invent speech from her. The school event supplied only a modest ethical lesson: an accusation can wound someone, so truth matters before repetition.

Akhlaq wanted to write the entire Qur’anic event as a comic scene in which he and Imaan stood beside Maryam. Dadi stopped him. “That would make you witnesses to a sacred history you did not live,” she said. “You can illustrate the lesson through your school’s actual fictional characters instead.”

The next morning the team took down the anonymous notice. With the teacher’s approval they posted a correction: THE CARDS WERE MOVED FOR LAMINATION. THE NEW STUDENT WAS NOT RESPONSIBLE. Akhlaq approached the pupil and apologised for having repeated what he had not checked. The pupil accepted the apology but said the whispers had made the morning difficult. Akhlaq listened rather than demanding immediate forgiveness.

Sheikh Uncle later read their new display card: DO NOT TURN UNCERTAINTY INTO AN ACCUSATION. He asked whether the children understood why that sentence belonged in a modern ethical lesson rather than as an invented part of the sacred account. They did.
For the first time the academy gallery contained a card that had cost them something: the courage to correct their own mistake.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Check facts, stop rumours and correct false accusations without demanding instant forgiveness.

The team had finished six large display panels, but Imaan felt the gallery still had no centre. The first panel explained Maryam’s honour, the second the glad tidings, and the third the importance of protecting truth. Yet visitors might leave remembering remarkable events without understanding the message taught by Prophet ʿĪsā.

Dadi Jaan opened Maryam 19:30–36 and asked Akhlaq to find the words that introduced ʿĪsā’s own status. He read the meaning of 19:30: ʿĪsā identified himself as the servant of Allah and a Prophet. The following verses mentioned prayer, giving and dutifulness to his mother. Verse 19:36 declared Allah the Lord of ʿĪsā and everyone else, and called people to worship Him.
“Then the centre is not a miracle picture,” Imaan said. “It is the truth about worship.”

At school Mohsin suggested a giant scoreboard: WHO IS THE MOST RIGHTEOUS PUPIL? He meant to encourage prayer and charity, but Sir Zameer explained that a score could count an answered question without knowing the sincerity of a person’s worship. Nor could any child be made to report private prayer or family circumstances to earn a prize.

They replaced the scoreboard with three quiet learning stations. At the first, pupils matched Qur’anic statements to their references. At the second, they chose a respectful response when someone asked about a different belief. At the third, they could select a voluntary act of service without telling the class what they had done.

During rehearsal, Akhlaq declared, “Anyone who does not agree with us must be shouted at!” Imaan looked startled. Sheikh Uncle corrected him: “We state Islamic belief faithfully and clearly, but we do not insult classmates or compel them to agree. Truthfulness does not require cruelty.”

Together they designed the centre panel: ʿĪSĀ (AS) — ALLAH’S SERVANT AND MESSENGER; WORSHIP ALLAH ALONE. The wording was theological, not a popularity contest, and the room remained welcoming to people who would learn respectfully.
That night Akhlaq sat beside Salaam after prayer. “The most important part of the story was not what people could see,” he said. “It was whom ʿĪsā taught them to worship.”

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Tawḥīd is taught clearly through worship, humility, prayer and everyday service.

stories.title: Signs Are Not Tricks
stories.subtitle: Miracles by Allah’s permission; kindness without false promises

blocks.text: Akhlaq was convinced that the fifth panel needed movement. “A mechanical bird!” he announced. “It will flap its wings when somebody presses a button.” Mohsin immediately wanted to make the bird fly over the visitors. Imaan remembered that the Qur’an describes signs given to ʿĪsā (AS), including a bird from clay becoming alive by Allah’s permission. She did not want anyone confusing a toy with a sacred miracle.

Sheikh Uncle read Āl ʿImrān 3:49 and explained the repeated words بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ — by Allah’s permission. The Qur’an also mentions the healing of people with serious illnesses and the raising of the dead, by Allah’s permission. None of these acts belonged to ordinary human skill, and a child could never unlock them through points or play.

Mohsin asked whether they should cancel every activity. “Not at all,” said Sir Zameer. “Teach the source with text, careful explanation and a neutral diagram. Then have a separate modern task that teaches responsible kindness.”

That afternoon the academy caretaker was absent through illness. Akhlaq wanted to promise the whole class that the caretaker would be well by Friday if everyone completed a kindness challenge. Salamah, who was helping prepare food for the family, explained that duʿāʾ and care are good, but nobody can guarantee a healing outcome or replace appropriate medical treatment with a game.

The team wrote a respectful card and asked the office whether practical help was needed. The answer was simple: keep the school hallway clear and ensure the substitute caretaker could reach the supplies. Akhlaq and Mohsin moved a box out of the walkway while Imaan prepared accurate labels for the exhibition.

They changed their panel title from AMAZING POWERS to SIGNS BY ALLAH’S PERMISSION. Underneath was a clear note: We do not imitate, simulate or score sacred miracles. Our practical lesson is to notice human needs and offer safe help.

When the caretaker returned the following week, the class welcomed him without asking for a dramatic report of his illness. For once, Akhlaq’s favourite part of the gallery was something ordinary: a clear path through which another person could walk.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Miracles belong to Allah’s permission; our duty is safe compassion and responsible care.

stories.title: The Helpers Who Stayed
stories.subtitle: Loyal service is not blind agreement

blocks.text: The evening before the exhibition, the academy team discovered that its recorded introduction had not saved correctly. The file opened, but there was only silence. Mohsin blamed the microphone. Akhlaq blamed the computer. Imaan asked the group to stop blaming one another long enough to find a solution.

Their sixth panel concerned Āl ʿImrān 3:52, where the disciples responded to ʿĪsā’s call for helpers in Allah’s cause. Sir Zameer had stressed that these were real followers in a sacred historical account, not roles for modern children to act out as a pretend scene from revelation. Their small class project could only practise the separate value of reliable cooperation.

There was less than an hour before the school closed. Mohsina checked the transcript. It was accurate and complete. Mohsin offered to re-record, Imaan held the printed text and Akhlaq checked the sound while Sir Zameer supervised. Nobody could repair the problem by claiming to have done every task alone.

Halfway through the recording, Akhlaq noticed a sentence that made it sound as though ʿĪsā performed miracles independently. He stopped the recording and pointed to the source. “We must say by Allah’s permission,” he reminded the others. Mohsin groaned at the delay. Then he looked at the screen and nodded. A faithful helper does not hide a mistake merely because correcting it costs time.

The corrected file was ready before closing. As they packed up, Sheikh Uncle asked how the group had behaved when pressured. Mohsina said they had listened. Mohsin said they had divided responsibilities. Imaan said they had checked their teaching. Akhlaq admitted he had enjoyed catching the error but had first wanted to boast about it.
The helpers of the Prophet belonged to sacred history. The children’s own duty was smaller, but real: help a truthful work without turning service into control or ego.
On the way home Akhlaq wrote in the gallery notebook: HELPFUL DOES NOT MEAN SILENT WHEN SOMETHING IS WRONG. It was the lesson their failed recording had finally taught them.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: A trustworthy helper checks truth, shares responsibility and corrects mistakes kindly.

stories.title: A Message for Those Who Come Later
stories.subtitle: Precise wording and truthful transmission

blocks.text: The last empty display frame was long and narrow. It reminded Akhlaq of a railway sign pointing toward a destination. He wanted to fill it with a list of every Prophet they had studied since the first world of ʿIBRAH Junior, but Imaan suggested that their present account included a special message for people who would come later.

Sheikh Uncle opened al-Ṣaff 61:6. ʿĪsā, son of Maryam, described himself as Allah’s Messenger to the Children of Israel, confirmed the Torah, and gave glad tidings of a Messenger to come after him named Aḥmad. The children learned that Muslims understand Aḥmad as a name of Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ. The source said this plainly; it did not require invented conversations or a fictional encounter between the two Prophets.

At the academy Sir Zameer showed the group a quotation that had been passed along in a class chat. It contained a beautiful sentence about helping others, but no reliable source. Some pupils wanted to put it under the name of Prophet ʿĪsā because the message sounded kind.

“Would it become true because it is kind?” asked Sir Zameer. Akhlaq looked down. He had forwarded quotations before without checking. Mohsina proposed leaving the statement unattributed until a qualified source could be found. Imaan suggested choosing a verified Qur’anic verse instead.

Together they made a new rule for the exhibition: if a line is from the Qur’an, label its sūrah and verse; if it is an explanation, name it as explanation; if it is modern fiction, call it fiction; if its origin is uncertain, do not attach a sacred name to it.

The final frame read: A MESSAGE OF TRUTH PASSES FORWARD WITH CARE. Beneath it stood the reference 61:6 and a short, accurate meaning guide. The group also prepared a small card describing the dignity of listening when someone asked about another faith, without mocking their beliefs or weakening the Islamic explanation.

That night Akhlaq told Dadi that messages could travel for years and still be spoiled by one careless person. “Then be a careful carrier,” she said. “Truth is too precious for decoration with false attributions.”

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Pass religious quotations on carefully; never assign sacred names to unverified statements.

stories.title: The Gallery Without a Final Picture
stories.subtitle: Allah’s protection, accountability and a living legacy

blocks.text: On opening day, the academy gallery was busy from the first hour. Parents visited the Qur’anic source panels, younger children listened to the narrated glossary, and older pupils tested themselves on evidence and applications. Only the final corner remained covered by a plain cloth.

Akhlaq was eager to reveal it, but Sir Zameer gathered the team first. “This last part is especially important,” he said. “We must not turn a difficult or contested sacred matter into a chase scene or an imaginary picture.” Dadi Jaan read the meanings of al-Nisāʾ 4:157–158: the Qur’an denies that ʿĪsā was killed or crucified and affirms that Allah raised him to Himself. It does not tell the children whom to draw as a substitute, how to dramatise a hidden event, or how to play the rescue as a game.

The next source panel referred to al-Māʾidah 5:116–117. On the Day of Judgment, ʿĪsā will affirm that he taught people to worship Allah, his Lord and their Lord. The children listened with seriousness. They understood that a complete Islamic account honours ʿĪsā greatly without treating him as divine.

When Akhlaq lifted the cloth, visitors saw no figure, no battle and no imagined scene. There were three large source cards: ALLAH’S PROTECTION. THE TRUTH ABOUT WORSHIP. OUR RESPONSIBILITY TO PASS THE MESSAGE ACCURATELY. Each card included its reference, followed by a separate ordinary-life activity.

An older pupil asked why there were no spectacular pictures at the end. Imaan answered that the Qur’an itself supplied what they could say with certainty. The goal was to understand revelation, not to fill its silences with whatever looked impressive. Mohsin nodded and said they had learned to be careful with stories, claims, promises and even their own teamwork.

After the guests departed, the children met around Dadi Jaan’s family table. They reviewed the eight lessons and chose one action each for the coming week. Mohsina chose to defend a classmate against rumours; Mohsin chose to check religious quotations; Imaan chose to help quietly; Akhlaq chose to ask before forwarding information.

Dadi closed the final folder. “The truthful account of a Prophet should make our own actions better,” she said. Akhlaq placed the folder beside the earlier worlds. The compass did not glow, but he no longer expected it to. The direction was already written in the guidance they had learned.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Honour the Qur’anic account, worship Allah alone and carry truthful character into action.

missions.title: Maryam Was Honoured

discover.text: Recognise Allah’s special honour of Maryam and resist unverified biographies or unfair comparisons.

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN

وَإِذْ قَالَتِ الْمَلَائِكَةُ يَا مَرْيَمُ إِنَّ اللَّهَ اصْطَفَاكِ وَطَهَّرَكِ وَاصْطَفَاكِ عَلَىٰ نِسَاءِ الْعَالَمِينَ

discover.text: Do I choose accurate learning over exciting guesses?

missions.question: A pupil proposes inventing a childhood story about Maryam to make a display more popular.

choices.text: Use the invented story because it sounds inspiring.
choices.feedback: Invented sacred stories cannot become historical truth simply because they attract attention. Revisit the evidence and try again.

choices.text: Teach the verified verse, label explanations, and avoid invented sacred scenes.
choices.feedback: Correct: verified revelation is our source boundary; fiction should be labelled separately. Give gentle explanation, show the source, and allow retry without penalty.

choices.text: Leave Maryam out entirely because not every detail is known.
choices.feedback: Lack of every detail does not mean we must omit what Allah explicitly told us. Revisit the evidence and try again.

missions.action: Read one verified fact about Maryam with a caregiver and mention its Qur’anic reference.

missions.question: The academy receives a donation and one child says every future problem is now solved.

choices.text: Refuse to celebrate because future problems are possible.

missions.title: Miracles by Allah’s Permission

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET
discover.text: Recognise that ʿĪsā’s miracles were signs from Allah, not abilities produced by tricks or app scores.

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN
discover.text: Āl ʿImrān, 3:49: ʿĪsā was sent to the Children of Israel with signs, including extraordinary healing and life-giving miracles solely by Allah’s permission.

وَرَسُولًا إِلَىٰ بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ أَنِّي قَدْ جِئْتُكُمْ بِآيَةٍ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ ۖ أَنِّي أَخْلُقُ لَكُمْ مِنَ الطِّينِ كَهَيْئَةِ الطَّيْرِ فَأَنْفُخُ فِيهِ فَيَكُونُ طَيْرًا بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ ۖ وَأُبْرِئُ الْأَكْمَهَ وَالْأَبْرَصَ وَأُحْيِي الْمَوْتَىٰ بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ ۖ وَأُنَبِّئُكُمْ بِمَا تَأْكُلُونَ وَمَا تَدَّخِرُونَ فِي بُيُوتِكُمْ ۚ إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَآيَةً لَكُمْ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: The signs given to ʿĪsā were divine miracles, repeatedly described as occurring by Allah’s permission. They cannot be reenacted or earned. This is the actual source boundary. The classroom situation below is an independent ethical application, not a scene from the Prophet’s life.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY

missions.question: The team plans a mechanical bird for an exhibit and wants to label it the miracle of ʿĪsā.

choices.text: Call the toy itself a miracle because it moves.

choices.text: Remove all explanation of the Qur’anic signs.
choices.feedback: The Qur’anic miracle must still be taught accurately through approved text. Revisit the evidence and try again.

choices.text: Use a text-only source panel about the miracle, and clearly label any toy as a modern mechanism.
choices.feedback: Correct: label technology as technology and explain the extraordinary sign separately. Give gentle explanation, show the source, and allow retry without penalty.

missions.action: Learn the meaning of “by Allah’s permission” and explain it carefully.

missions.question: A group recording contains a mistaken religious phrase shortly before the deadline.

choices.text: Correct it respectfully, check the source and share the tasks fairly.

missions.title: A Message of Aḥmad

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET
discover.text: Recognise ʿĪsā’s glad tidings of the Messenger Aḥmad, understood as Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ, and practise accurate attribution.

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN
discover.text: Al-Ṣaff, 61:6: ʿĪsā confirmed the Torah and gave glad tidings of a messenger after him named Aḥmad.

وَإِذْ قَالَ عِيسَى ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ يَا بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ إِنِّي رَسُولُ اللَّهِ إِلَيْكُمْ مُصَدِّقًا لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيَّ مِنَ التَّوْرَاةِ وَمُبَشِّرًا بِرَسُولٍ يَأْتِي مِنْ بَعْدِي اسْمُهُ أَحْمَدُ ۖ فَلَمَّا جَاءَهُمْ بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ قَالُوا هَٰذَا سِحْرٌ مُبِينٌ

discover.label: Complete working āyah
discover.text: verified Arabic and licensed translation required in the production app.

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: ʿĪsā announced a messenger named Aḥmad, understood in Islam as Muḥammad ﷺ. Accuracy in transmitting religious teaching is part of respect. This is the actual source boundary. The classroom situation below is an independent ethical application, not a scene from the Prophet’s life.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY
discover.text: Do I attach sacred names to quotations I have not verified?

missions.question: Someone forwards a beautiful line and asks you to publish it as a saying of ʿĪsā without evidence.

choices.text: Publish it with his name because it is beautiful.
choices.feedback: An attractive sentence is not automatically an authentic Prophetic quotation. Revisit the evidence and try again.

choices.text: Change it into a miracle story to make it memorable.
choices.feedback: Adding miracles to unverified speech creates further false history. Revisit the evidence and try again.

choices.text: Check with a reliable source; if unverified, do not attribute it to the Prophet.
choices.feedback: Correct: check the source; do not attribute uncertain material to Prophets. Give gentle explanation, show the source, and allow retry without penalty.

missions.action: Check the source of one quotation before forwarding it.

missions.title: Allah Raised ʿĪsā

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET
discover.text: State the Qur’anic account accurately without inventing a crucifixion or escape scene or playing out violence.

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN
discover.text: Al-Nisāʾ, 4:158: Rather, Allah raised ʿĪsā to Himself; Allah is Almighty and Wise.
بَلْ رَفَعَهُ اللَّهُ إِلَيْهِ ۚ وَكَانَ اللَّهُ عَزِيزًا حَكِيمًا

discover.label: Complete working āyah
discover.text: verified Arabic and licensed translation required in the production app.

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: The Qur’an rejects his being killed or crucified in 4:157 and affirms that Allah raised him to Himself in 4:158. Do not invent the unseen details. This is the actual source boundary. The classroom situation below is an independent ethical application, not a scene from the Prophet’s life.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY
discover.text: Do I fill in an unknown sacred detail simply to make a story exciting?

missions.question: The group wants to include an action game showing how ʿĪsā escaped his enemies.

choices.text: Invent a chase and let players decide his fate.
choices.feedback: An action game would invent details the Qur’an did not state. Revisit the evidence and try again.

choices.text: Show the verses and explain that Allah raised him, without depicting the event or adding a substitute identity.
choices.feedback: Correct: teach 4:157–158 clearly and do not portray the unseen event. Give gentle explanation, show the source, and allow retry without penalty.

choices.text: Tell the class that the Qur’an confirms his crucifixion.
choices.feedback: The Qur’an explicitly rejects crucifixion and confirms that Allah raised him. Revisit the evidence and try again.

missions.action: Identify Qur’an 4:157–158 and explain its core teaching in one careful sentence.

missions.title: The One Lord We Worship

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET
discover.text: Explain that ʿĪsā taught worship of Allah alone and that every person is responsible for truthful conduct.

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN
discover.text: Al-Māʾidah, 5:117: On the Day of Judgment ʿĪsā will affirm that he only instructed people to worship Allah, his Lord and their Lord.

مَا قُلْتُ لَهُمْ إِلَّا مَا أَمَرْتَنِي بِهِ أَنِ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ رَبِّي وَرَبَّكُمْ ۚ وَكُنْتُ عَلَيْهِمْ شَهِيدًا مَا دُمْتُ فِيهِمْ ۖ فَلَمَّا تَوَفَّيْتَنِي كُنْتَ أَنْتَ الرَّقِيبَ عَلَيْهِمْ ۚ وَأَنْتَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ شَهِيدٌ

discover.label: Complete working āyah
discover.text: verified Arabic and licensed translation required in the production app.

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: ʿĪsā will affirm that he taught worship of Allah, his Lord and the Lord of all people. Muslim children can state this respectfully and clearly. This is the actual source boundary. The classroom situation below is an independent ethical application, not a scene from the Prophet’s life.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY
discover.text: What truthful action will I carry forward this week?

missions.question: An exhibition visitor asks what Muslims believe ʿĪsā taught about worship.

choices.text: Insult other religions rather than explaining the verse.
choices.feedback: Insulting others is unacceptable and avoids the actual Qur’anic answer. Revisit the evidence and try again.

choices.text: Say the Qur’an asks people to worship ʿĪsā himself.
choices.feedback: The Qur’an teaches worship of Allah alone, not worship of ʿĪsā. Revisit the evidence and try again.

choices.text: Explain that he called people to worship Allah, his Lord and their Lord, with respectful language.
choices.feedback: Correct: state the Islamic teaching faithfully with courtesy. Give gentle explanation, show the source, and allow retry without penalty.

remember.label: Vocabulary
remember.text: اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ — worship Allah; رَبِّي وَرَبَّكُمْ — my Lord and your Lord

review.arabic: وَإِذْ قَالَتِ الْمَلَائِكَةُ يَا مَرْيَمُ إِنَّ اللَّهَ اصْطَفَاكِ وَطَهَّرَكِ وَاصْطَفَاكِ عَلَىٰ نِسَاءِ الْعَالَمِينَ
review.meaning: Allah chose and purified Maryam and honoured her above the women of the worlds.

review.arabic: إِذْ قَالَتِ الْمَلَائِكَةُ يَا مَرْيَمُ إِنَّ اللَّهَ يُبَشِّرُكِ بِكَلِمَةٍ مِنْهُ اسْمُهُ الْمَسِيحُ عِيسَى ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ وَجِيهًا فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ وَمِنَ الْمُقَرَّبِينَ
review.meaning: Maryam received glad tidings of the Messiah, ʿĪsā son of Maryam, honoured in this life and the next.

review.arabic: قَالَتْ رَبِّ أَنَّىٰ يَكُونُ لِي وَلَدٌ وَلَمْ يَمْسَسْنِي بَشَرٌ ۖ قَالَ كَذَٰلِكِ اللَّهُ يَخْلُقُ مَا يَشَاءُ ۚ إِذَا قَضَىٰ أَمْرًا فَإِنَّمَا يَقُولُ لَهُ كُنْ فَيَكُونُ
review.meaning: Maryam asked how she could have a child without a man having touched her; Allah creates whatever He wills.

review.arabic: قَالَ كَذَٰلِكِ قَالَ رَبُّكِ هُوَ عَلَيَّ هَيِّنٌ ۖ وَلِنَجْعَلَهُ آيَةً لِلنَّاسِ وَرَحْمَةً مِنَّا ۚ وَكَانَ أَمْرًا مَقْضِيًّا
review.meaning: The extraordinary birth was easy for Allah and would be a sign for people and mercy from Him.

review.arabic: قَالَ إِنِّي عَبْدُ اللَّهِ آتَانِيَ الْكِتَابَ وَجَعَلَنِي نَبِيًّا
review.meaning: The infant ʿĪsā spoke by Allah’s miracle, declaring himself Allah’s servant and a prophet.

review.arabic: وَجَعَلَنِي مُبَارَكًا أَيْنَ مَا كُنْتُ وَأَوْصَانِي بِالصَّلَاةِ وَالزَّكَاةِ مَا دُمْتُ حَيًّا
review.meaning: Allah made ʿĪsā blessed and commanded prayer and giving throughout his life.

review.arabic: وَبَرًّا بِوَالِدَتِي وَلَمْ يَجْعَلْنِي جَبَّارًا شَقِيًّا
review.meaning: Allah made ʿĪsā dutiful to his mother, not arrogant or miserable.

review.arabic: وَالسَّلَامُ عَلَيَّ يَوْمَ وُلِدْتُ وَيَوْمَ أَمُوتُ وَيَوْمَ أُبْعَثُ حَيًّا
review.meaning: ʿĪsā spoke of peace at his birth, future death, and resurrection; this is not a claim that he was crucified.

review.arabic: ذَٰلِكَ عِيسَى ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ ۚ قَوْلَ الْحَقِّ الَّذِي فِيهِ يَمْتَرُونَ
review.meaning: This is ʿĪsā, son of Maryam, the truthful account about which people dispute.

review.arabic: وَإِنَّ اللَّهَ رَبِّي وَرَبُّكُمْ فَاعْبُدُوهُ ۚ هَٰذَا صِرَاطٌ مُسْتَقِيمٌ
review.meaning: Allah is the Lord of ʿĪsā and of all people, and He alone is to be worshipped.

review.arabic: وَرَسُولًا إِلَىٰ بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ أَنِّي قَدْ جِئْتُكُمْ بِآيَةٍ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ ۖ أَنِّي أَخْلُقُ لَكُمْ مِنَ الطِّينِ كَهَيْئَةِ الطَّيْرِ فَأَنْفُخُ فِيهِ فَيَكُونُ طَيْرًا بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ ۖ وَأُبْرِئُ الْأَكْمَهَ وَالْأَبْرَصَ وَأُحْيِي الْمَوْتَىٰ بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ ۖ وَأُنَبِّئُكُمْ بِمَا تَأْكُلُونَ وَمَا تَدَّخِرُونَ فِي بُيُوتِكُمْ ۚ إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَآيَةً لَكُمْ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ
review.meaning: ʿĪsā was sent to the Children of Israel with signs, including extraordinary healing and life-giving miracles solely by Allah’s permission.

review.arabic: فَلَمَّا أَحَسَّ عِيسَىٰ مِنْهُمُ الْكُفْرَ قَالَ مَنْ أَنْصَارِي إِلَى اللَّهِ ۖ قَالَ الْحَوَارِيُّونَ نَحْنُ أَنْصَارُ اللَّهِ آمَنَّا بِاللَّهِ وَاشْهَدْ بِأَنَّا مُسْلِمُونَ
review.meaning: When ʿĪsā called for helpers in Allah’s cause, the disciples affirmed their faith and submission to Allah.

review.arabic: وَإِذْ قَالَ عِيسَى ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ يَا بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ إِنِّي رَسُولُ اللَّهِ إِلَيْكُمْ مُصَدِّقًا لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيَّ مِنَ التَّوْرَاةِ وَمُبَشِّرًا بِرَسُولٍ يَأْتِي مِنْ بَعْدِي اسْمُهُ أَحْمَدُ ۖ فَلَمَّا جَاءَهُمْ بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ قَالُوا هَٰذَا سِحْرٌ مُبِينٌ
review.meaning: ʿĪsā confirmed the Torah and gave glad tidings of a messenger after him named Aḥmad.

review.arabic: وَقَوْلِهِمْ إِنَّا قَتَلْنَا الْمَسِيحَ عِيسَى ابْنَ مَرْيَمَ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ وَمَا صَلَبُوهُ وَلَٰكِنْ شُبِّهَ لَهُمْ ۚ وَإِنَّ الَّذِينَ اخْتَلَفُوا فِيهِ لَفِي شَكٍّ مِنْهُ ۚ مَا لَهُمْ بِهِ مِنْ عِلْمٍ إِلَّا اتِّبَاعَ الظَّنِّ ۚ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًا
review.meaning: The Qur’an explicitly rejects the claim that ʿĪsā was killed or crucified.

review.arabic: بَلْ رَفَعَهُ اللَّهُ إِلَيْهِ ۚ وَكَانَ اللَّهُ عَزِيزًا حَكِيمًا
review.meaning: Rather, Allah raised ʿĪsā to Himself; Allah is Almighty and Wise.

review.arabic: مَا قُلْتُ لَهُمْ إِلَّا مَا أَمَرْتَنِي بِهِ أَنِ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ رَبِّي وَرَبَّكُمْ ۚ وَكُنْتُ عَلَيْهِمْ شَهِيدًا مَا دُمْتُ فِيهِمْ ۖ فَلَمَّا تَوَفَّيْتَنِي كُنْتَ أَنْتَ الرَّقِيبَ عَلَيْهِمْ ۚ وَأَنْتَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ شَهِيدٌ
review.meaning: On the Day of Judgment ʿĪsā will affirm that he only instructed people to worship Allah, his Lord and their Lord.

synthesis.text: Maryam’s honour and the birth of ʿĪsā

Āl ʿImrān 3:42–47 and Maryam 19:16–21 honour Maryam and describe the extraordinary birth of ʿĪsā without a father, by Allah’s creative power. His birth is a sign and mercy, not a reason to invent intimate historical details or to promise that ordinary families can obtain a comparable miracle. The children’s practical lessons are respect, careful source use, gratitude and the courage to ask responsible questions.
Allah’s servant and Messenger: the centre of Tawḥīd

Maryam 19:30–36 clearly presents ʿĪsā as Allah’s servant and a Prophet, commanded to prayer, giving and dutifulness toward his mother. His message is worship of Allah alone. The Islamic teaching that he is neither Allah nor Allah’s son is a doctrinal foundation, not an optional interfaith revision; at the same time, every class discussion must respect human dignity and forbid religious ridicule. The student learns to explain truth without arrogance.
Miracles by Allah’s permission

Āl ʿImrān 3:49 and al-Māʾidah 5:110 repeatedly attach his miracles to Allah’s permission. Neither an app, a gadget, a child’s duʿāʾ nor a reward score gives humans such powers. A child’s real opportunities are compassion, appropriate medical help, safe service and truthfulness about outcomes. No miraculous event is displayed as a playable experience, and no child is blamed for an illness remaining unresolved.
Reliable helpers, true transmission and the next Messenger

Āl ʿImrān 3:52 describes the disciples’ declared help and faith. Al-Ṣaff 61:6 records ʿĪsā giving glad tidings of a messenger named Aḥmad, understood as Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ. The modern educational applications are careful cooperation, source-checked religious quotations and the willingness to correct an error even when inconvenient. The disciples’ sacred identity is not an app costume or role.
Allah’s raising of ʿĪsā and the Day of Judgment

Al-Nisāʾ 4:157–158 rejects that ʿĪsā was killed or crucified and affirms that Allah raised him. The Qur’an does not identify a substitute for children to draw or stage. Authentic Hadith discuss his return before the Hour; any expanded treatment must be specifically sourced and age reviewed. Al-Māʾidah 5:116–117 teaches that ʿĪsā will reject false worship and affirm that he called people to worship Allah alone. This gives the volume a lasting ending: honour the Prophet by holding to the truth he taught.
CARRY FORWARD • Love and honour ʿĪsā (AS), worship Allah alone, verify religious knowledge, defend people from false accusations, serve with compassion, and tell the truth with dignity.
Seven-day voluntary family practice programme
Day
Small practical action
Private reflection
Read one verified Qur’anic statement about Maryam and identify its source.
Did I distinguish a true reference from a guess?
Thank someone for a genuine kindness without promising the future.
Was my gratitude truthful?
Pause before repeating a claim and correct any unfair rumour.
Did I protect another person’s dignity?
Read Maryam 19:30–36 with an adult and discuss worship of Allah alone.
Can I explain Tawḥīd kindly?
Choose one safe, voluntary act of care for a person in need.
Did I ask what help would be useful?
Check one religious quotation or source before sharing.
Was the attribution accurate?
Recall 4:157–158 and 5:117; choose one good habit to carry forward.
What truth and character practice will continue?
Closing family and educator conversation
What does the Qur’an tell us about Maryam, and which details should not be invented?
How can we explain the extraordinary birth of ʿĪsā without making inaccurate promises about everyday life?
Why is the phrase “by Allah’s permission” essential when speaking about ʿĪsā’s miracles?
How do prayer, giving, kindness to a mother and Tawḥīd appear together in Maryam 19:30–36?
How can we state Islamic teaching about ʿĪsā respectfully when classmates have different beliefs?
What source-checking habit and compassionate action will our family keep practising?
